coreTruths.title: Caries is a dynamic balance between demineralisation and remineralisation, not one-way decay
coreTruths.broaderContext: Caries is one of the two great causes of tooth loss. Treating it as a balance rather than a slope changes the whole logic of restorative dentistry.
coreTruths.body:
## The tooth surface is in constant flux

Every sugar hit drops plaque pH and pulls calcium and phosphate out of enamel. When pH rises, those ions diffuse back in. Caries is the running tally of those swings, not a one-way slide [1].

## A white spot is a moment of decision, not a reason to drill

A white spot lesion is demineralisation in the sub-surface layer with the surface still intact. Tip the balance, with fluoride, less sugar, better cleaning, and the lesion can stall and even regress [2]. Once it cavitates, the option to arrest is gone and prevention has to be paired with restoration [3].

## Telling the patient the lesion can still arrest changes the consultation

The message that an early lesion has the potential to arrest is what makes preventive advice land. It moves the patient from passive recipient to someone who can change the outcome [4]. A preventive philosophy on the dentist's part, giving early lesions the chance to arrest before reaching for the bur, is as important as preventing new ones [5].

citations.quote: Caries is ∴ a dynamic process characterized by episodic demineralization and remineralization occurring over time.
Under favourable conditions a lesion may become inactive and even regress.
Pre-cavitated lesion—prevention. Cavitated lesion—prevention and restoration.

Counsel the patient that if the lesion is not cavitated, it has the potential to arrest. This makes the preventive advice very relevant to the patient, increasing the chance of that patient acting on the advice.

Of equal importance with the prevention of new lesions is a preventive philosophy on the part of the dentist, so that early carious lesions are given the chance to arrest and a minimalistic approach is taken to the excision of caries where 1° prevention has failed.

coreTruths.title: Fluoride works mainly topically and post-eruptively, not by being baked into developing enamel
coreTruths.broaderContext: Fluoride is the single most powerful caries preventive in dentistry. Knowing it works topically, not systemically, is what makes daily toothpaste advice the centrepiece of prevention.
coreTruths.body:
## Frequent low-concentration topical exposure beats systemic dosing

The biggest action of fluoride is favouring remineralisation of the early lesion. Pre-eruptive incorporation does something, but most of the benefit comes from frequent low-concentration topical exposure [1]. That is why a tube of toothpaste used twice a day matters more than any prenatal supplement.

## Newly erupted teeth get the most benefit

Fluoride inhibits demineralisation, drives remineralisation, and slows acid production by plaque bacteria. Newly erupted teeth pick up the most protection [2]. So the years right after eruption are when fluoride exposure pays the highest dividend.

## The toothpaste rules are the practical core

Brush twice daily with at least 1000ppm fluoride toothpaste, or 1350-1500ppm for those over 3 or at higher caries risk [3]. Smear under 3, pea-sized blob over 3 [4]. Spit, do not rinse, so fluoride stays on the tooth [5]. Parents supervise to at least 7 to limit ingestion and ensure plaque actually comes off [6].

## Varnish is the in-clinic top-up

Duraphat varnish at 22,600ppm is applied two to four times a year to children over 3 deemed at risk, and is the most evidence-backed in-clinic fluoride [7]. It is contraindicated in asthma and is used carefully in young children given the high concentration [7].

## Toxicity is a real but bounded risk

The safely tolerated dose is about 1mg F/kg, the dose that warrants hospitalisation is 5mg F/kg [8]. A 5-year-old at 19kg would need to swallow about 63mL of 1500ppm toothpaste to hit that threshold [9], which is why the smear/pea rule matters but the everyday tube is not a poisoning risk.

citations.quote: The most important action of fluoride is to favour remineralization of the early carious lesion. Although fluoride incorporated within developing enamel results in a high local concentration following acid attack, the maximum benefit appears to be derived from frequent low-concentration topical administration.
NB: newly erupted teeth derive the most benefit.
Brush twice daily (bd) with a >1000ppm fluoride toothpaste. >3yrs and those at ↑ risk of developing caries use 1350–1500ppm fluoride toothpaste.
Children <3yrs of age should use a ‘smear’ and >3yrs a small pea-size blob (<0.3mL) of toothpaste.
Spit out well, but do not rinse, after brushing.

Brushing with fluoride toothpaste should start as soon as the first teeth erupt (about 6 months of age). Parents should supervise brushing up to at least 7yrs of age to avoid over-ingestion of toothpaste and ensure adequate plaque removal.

Fluoride varnish has been shown to be effective in ↓ caries incidence in children, and regular application (two times per year ↑ to three or four times per year where caries risk is i) is now advocated for all children over age 3yrs deemed to be at risk of caries. However, it should be applied carefully and sparingly, especially in young children as it contains 22,600ppm fluoride. Application of Duraphat® varnish is C/I in patients suffering from asthma.

Safely tolerated dose (STD). Dose below which symptoms of toxicity are unlikely = 1mg/kg body weight. Potentially lethal dose (PLD). Lowest dose associated with a fatality. Patient should be hospitalized = 5mg/kg body weight.
To reach the 5mg F/kg threshold (requiring hospitalization) a 5yr-old (about 19kg) would have to ingest 95 (1mg F) tablets, 63mL of 1500ppm toothpaste, or 7.6mL of 1.23% of APF gel.

coreTruths.title: Saliva is a built-in caries defence; lose it and most of the other defences fall over
coreTruths.broaderContext: Saliva is the mouth's antacid, ion reservoir, and antibacterial coat. The dry mouth patient sits at the centre of why caries risk assessment exists at all.
coreTruths.body:
## Saliva does three jobs at once

Saliva acts as an oral antacid through its alkaline pH at high flow and its buffering capacity [1]. It cuts plaque accumulation and clears foodstuffs [2]. It keeps a reservoir of calcium, phosphate, and fluoride sitting around the tooth so remineralisation has the raw materials it needs [3]. And it is mildly antibacterial through IgA, lysozyme, lactoferrin, and lactoperoxidase [4].

## The dry mouth patient teaches the lesson

Looking at a patient with xerostomia is the fastest way to appreciate what saliva does [5]. Caries races, root surfaces give way, and standard preventive advice has to be ratcheted up. These are the patients who get fluoride varnish more often, chlorhexidine when plaque is hard to control, and stricter dietary counselling.

## Stimulating saliva is a small but real lever

Chewing sugar-free gum after meals stimulates saliva and gives a small reduction in caries [6]. Foods that stimulate flow, cheese, sugar-free gum, salted peanuts, can speed the return of plaque pH to normal after a sugar hit [7]. Useful add-on advice, not a replacement for the basics.

citations.quote: Saliva acts as an IO antacid, due to its alkaline pH at high flow rates and buffering capacity.
↓ plaque accumulation and aids clearance of foodstuffs.
Acts as a reservoir of calcium, phosphate, and fluoride ions, thereby favouring remineralization.
Has an antibacterial action because of its IgA, lysozyme, lactoferrin, and lactoperoxidase content.
An appreciation of the importance of saliva can be gained by examining a patient with a dry mouth.
Chewing sugar-free gum regularly after meals stimulates saliva production and does appear to ↓ caries, but the reduction is small.
Foods that stimulate salivary flow can speed the return of plaque pH to normal (e.g. cheese, sugar-free gum, salted peanuts).

coreTruths.title: Caries is a sugar-frequency disease, not a sugar-amount disease
coreTruths.broaderContext: Sugar drives caries, but it's the number of acid attacks per day that matters most. This reframes dietary advice from total restriction to changing when sugar is eaten.
coreTruths.body:
## Frequency, not just quantity, drives the lesion

The frequency of sugary intakes and the gap between them, total sugar in the diet, concentration, and stickiness all matter [1]. Each exposure pushes plaque pH below the critical line. Six small sugar hits across a day cause more demineralisation than one big sugar bolus at a meal.

## Sucrose is the worst, but other sugars cause caries too

Sucrose sits at the top of the cariogenicity list, partly because plaque turns it into the extracellular polysaccharide that helps plaque stick [2]. Glucose, fructose, maltose, then galactose and lactose, all follow [3]. Fruit-based drinks, including the no-added-sugar ones, are a key driver of early childhood caries [2].

## Practical advice is built around frequency

The core message: cut frequency of sugar-containing foods and drinks, especially between meals [4]. Cut frequency of fruit-based drinks even when labelled no-added-sugar [5]. Save sweets for one occasion or the end of a meal rather than spreading them across the day [6]. An all-in-one chocolate bar beats a packet of individual sweets [7].

## Watch the indirect harms of "safe" snacks

Nuts, cheese, and crisps are dentally safer between-meal snacks but high in fat, and peanuts can be inhaled by small children [8]. Diet colas are sugar free but still erosive [8]. Dental advice has to sit inside general health advice, not contradict it [9].

citations.quote: The frequency of sugary intakes and the interval between them, the total amount of sugar eaten in the diet, and the concentration of sugar and stickiness of a food have been shown to be important.

Sucrose is considered a major culprit—it is the most commonly available sugar and able to facilitate production of extracellular polysaccharide in plaque. However, other sugars can also cause caries, e.g. frequent consumption of fruit-based drinks is known to be a key factor in the development of early childhood caries (ECC).
Sucrose, glucose, fructose, maltose. Galactose, lactose. Complex carbohydrate (e.g. starch in rice, bread, potatoes).
Reduce frequency of consumption of sugar-containing foods and drinks, especially between meals.
Reduce frequency of consumption of fruit-based drinks, even those labelled ‘no added sugar’.
Save sweets to be eaten on 1 day, e.g. Saturday dinnertime, or to be eaten at the end of a meal.
All-in-one chocolate bars are preferable to packets of individual sweets.

But remember that while cheese, peanuts, and crisps may constitute a safe snack in dental terms, they are all high in fat, and peanuts can be inhaled by small children. Also, ‘diet’ cola drinks are sugar free, but can still cause erosion if large quantities are drunk.

Therefore, dental dietary advice should be given in the wider context of the general health of the individual, i.e. ↓ consumption of sugars and fats, and ↑ consumption of fibre-rich starchy foods, fresh fruit, and vegetables. Meals provide a better nutritional balance than snacks. Hence, good eating/drinking at mealtimes and avoiding between-meals snacking is healthy.

coreTruths.title: Fissure sealants exist because brushing and fluoride can't reach pit-and-fissure caries
coreTruths.broaderContext: Fluoride works best on smooth surfaces; pits and fissures are physically protected from both bristle and saliva. Sealants close the gap that prevention otherwise leaves open.
coreTruths.body:
## Fissures are a niche brushing can't reach

Pits and fissures shelter bacteria that toothbrush bristles are too wide to clean out [1]. Fluoride is more effective on smooth surface caries than fissure caries [2]. As fluoride has driven down approximal decay, occlusal lesions are now relatively more important, which is why sealants matter even more than before [3].

## Target sealants by risk, not by routine

Seal first molars in children with extensive primary-dentition caries (dmf surfaces 2 or more) and in children with impairments [4]. Caries-free primary dentitions do not need routine sealing of 6s, just monitoring [5]. If one 6 has occlusal caries, seal the rest of the caries-free permanent molars [6].

## Seal as soon as moisture control allows

Newly erupted first molars get the biggest benefit, but they are also the hardest to keep dry [7]. Aim to seal within two years of eruption [7]. Glass ionomer is a temporary holder when isolation is impossible, for example partially erupted teeth or poor cooperation, until resin can be placed [8].

## A stained fissure is a decision point

If a stained fissure is questionable, take a bitewing. Lesion in enamel: seal and monitor [9]. Lesion into dentine: preventive resin restoration unless the cavity exceeds a third of the occlusal, in which case go conventional [9]. Sealants reduce dentine caries incidence by over 50% over four years and need monitoring with replenishment of any defects [10].

citations.quote: Pits and fissures provide a sheltered niche for bacterial proliferation. Toothbrush bristles are too wide to fit into these areas, making complete plaque removal impossible. A fissure sealant (f/s) is a material that provides an impervious barrier to the fissure system to prevent the development of caries.
NB: fluoride is more effective in reducing smooth surface than pit and fissure caries.

In developed countries, the ↓ in caries seen in recent years has not been uniform for all tooth surfaces. Part of this ↓ is due to an ↑ availability of fluoride, leading to a greater reduction in approximal, rather than in pit and fissure caries. Therefore, the need for a method of preventing occlusal caries is even more pressing.
F/s should be provided for 6s in: children with impairments. those with extensive caries in the 1° dentition (decayed, missing, filled surfaces index is 2 or more).
Children with caries-free 1° dentitions do not need routine f/s of 6s but should be monitored regularly. F/s of 1° molars is not normally recommended.
Where occlusal caries affects one 6, the remaining caries-free permanent molars (6s and 7s) should be f/s.

To be effective, f/s need to be carefully applied to susceptible teeth. They are most valuable in recently erupted (especially first) molars, but moisture control may be difficult. Therefore, sealants should be monitored and replaced if lost. For maximum benefit, teeth should be sealed as soon as practicable after eruption and certainly within 2yrs.

GI sealants do release fluoride but have poorer retention than resin sealants. They are useful for high caries-risk children as a temporary sealant where adequate isolation for successful placement of resin-based sealants is not possible, e.g. partially erupted teeth/poor cooperation.

If there is doubt about a stained fissure, a b/w radiograph should be taken. If the lesion is in enamel, f/s and monitor clinically and radiographically. If in doubt, carry out an enamel biopsy. If the lesion extends to dentine place a preventive resin restoration (PRR), providing the cavity does not extend to more than one-third of the occlusal surface, in which case a conventional restoration is required.
A f/s is highly effective and reduces the incidence of dentine caries over 4yrs by >50%.

coreTruths.title: Toothbrushing prevents caries chiefly as a fluoride-delivery vehicle, not by mechanical plaque removal alone
coreTruths.broaderContext: Brushing is the most repeated preventive act in dentistry. Understanding that its caries benefit comes from the fluoride it carries, not the wiping, sharpens what gets emphasised in OHI.
coreTruths.body:
## Brushing alone does not prevent caries

The evidence is uncomfortable: toothbrushing alone is not an effective method of caries control [1]. The reason brushing works is that it spreads fluoride toothpaste across teeth twice a day. Take the fluoride out of the equation and the mechanical action does little for caries.

## Brushing still does prevent gingivitis and periodontitis

The same brushing that disappoints on caries does succeed on gum disease. Long-term plaque control gives much less oral disease overall, including less caries, but the strongest signal is on gingivitis [1]. So OHI gets framed two ways: brushing protects the gums, the fluoride in the toothpaste protects the teeth.

## Chemical plaque control has a niche

Chlorhexidine 0.2% mouthwash and 1% gel reduce caries when used regularly, but staining, taste disturbance, and parotid swelling limit routine use [2]. The real role is in patients who can't physically brush well, those with disabilities or reduced salivary flow [2]. It is also inactivated by toothpaste, so timing matters [2].

## The unifying message stays simple

The four-line public message has stood up: restrict sugar to mealtimes, brush twice daily with fluoride toothpaste, attend regularly, water fluoridation is beneficial [3]. Keep the message simple, repeat it, and tailor it to the patient. Too much detail backfires [4].

citations.quote: By the individual. The available evidence suggests that toothbrushing alone is not an effective method of caries control. However, a long-term study has demonstrated much less oral disease, including dental caries, in patients who maintain good plaque control over many years. Also ↓ gingivitis.

To achieve more than a transitory effect, an antiseptic needs to be retained in the mouth. Chlorhexidine, a positively charged bactericidal and fungicidal antiseptic, is capable of this. It is attracted to the negatively charged proteins on the surface of teeth and oral mucosa and in saliva from where it gradually leaches out. It is available as a 0.2% mouthwash and a 1% gel which are cheaper over the counter than by prescription. Although the main application of chlorhexidine is in the management of gingivitis, it has been shown to be effective at ↓ caries when used regularly. While its widespread use for this purpose is not practical, it can be helpful in the management of disabled patients or those with ↓ salivary flow. Unwanted effects include staining, disturbance of taste, and parotid swelling (which is reversible). It is less effective in the presence of a large build-up of plaque and is inactivated by commercial toothpastes.
Restrict sugar-containing foods to mealtimes. Clean teeth and gums thoroughly bd with a fluoride toothpaste. Attend the dentist regularly. Water fluoridation is beneficial.
Relevant to the individual, their lifestyle and problems. Keep the message simple. Too much information may be counter-productive. Repetition of message. Positive reinforcement.

coreTruths.title: Whether dental advice gets followed depends as much on access, anxiety, and class as on the advice itself
coreTruths.broaderContext: Prevention only works if people show up and act on it. Anxiety, cost, geography, and social class are why the same advice produces different outcomes across the population.
coreTruths.body:
## Anxiety and cost are the two biggest barriers

The two main barriers to regular dental attendance are anxiety and cost [1]. Anxiety shows up as fear of pain, fear of a particular procedure, or just a feeling of vulnerability from giving up control [2]. The reception staff and the waiting environment shape first impressions before the dentist has said a word [2]. The dentist's own manner, friendly, personal, explaining what is coming, can either calm or stoke that anxiety [2].

## Cost is often more about confusion than amount

Many patients believe dentistry is expensive and find the charging system confusing. A clear estimate before treatment is reassuring [3]. The clinical fix here is communication, not discount.

## Geography and social class are silent multipliers

Dentists cluster in leafy suburbs more than in poor inner cities, and a high dentist-to-population ratio drives higher attendance [4]. Social class affects both incidence of dental disease and uptake of dental care [5]. Notably, the social class gap in caries narrows in fluoridated areas [5]. Public-health prevention reaches groups that individual education does not.

## Attendance changes through life

Children now mostly enjoy a visit. Adolescents drop the habit through apathy or competing pressures. Pregnancy, wanting to set an example for kids, or fear of becoming edentulous can pull adults back [6]. Knowing the life-stage pattern helps target recall reminders that actually land.

## Recall is risk-based, not six-monthly by default

NICE recommends recall intervals based on individual risk: 3-24 months for adults, 3-12 months for children [7]. There is no clear benefit to under-12-monthly recall in healthy patients, but at-risk patients need to be seen more often [8]. A child's first check-up is once the first teeth erupt, usually between 6 months and 1 year [9].

citations.quote: Aside from the problems experienced by patients accessing NHS dental care, research has shown that the two main barriers to regular uptake of dental care by the general public are anxiety and cost.

This manifests as fear of pain or a particular procedure, or a feeling of vulnerability brought about by relinquishing control to the dentist in the sensitive area of the mouth. A patient’s first impressions are important as the reception they receive from staff and the environment in which they wait to be seen could either allay or reinforce their anxieties. The attitude of the dentist is also a significant factor: a ‘good’ dentist has a friendly, personal touch and explains what Rx is going to involve.
The perception still exists that dental Rx is expensive. Patients often find the way in which the charges are calculated confusing but welcome an estimate of the costs prior to Rx.

Availability and accessibility of dental services. Research shows that a greater proportion of the public visit the dentist regularly where the dentist-to-population ratio is high. This ratio tends to follow a geographical pattern, with the greatest number of dentists in the south-east.

Social class affects both the incidence of dental disease and the uptake of dental care. Interestingly, the differences in caries experience between the social classes are much lower in fluoridated regions.

Furthermore, the pattern of attendance varies throughout life, with children now enjoying a visit to the dentist, but adolescents breaking the habit of regular attendance due to apathy &/or other pressures on their time. A return to the dentist may be triggered by pregnancy and desire to provide a good example to the children, or a need for urgent Rx and a fear of becoming edentulous.

In the UK, guidance from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommends that dental recall intervals (‘oral health review’ intervals) should be determined by the needs of the individual patient based on a risk assessment of existing disease progressing or new disease developing. For adult patients this interval can be between 3 and 24 months and for children 3 and 12 months.
The available evidence suggests that there is no clear benefit for recall intervals of <1yr for healthy patients, although the at-risk patient often needs to be seen more frequently.
A child’s first check-up should occur once the first teeth have erupted (i.e. usually between 6 months and 1yr of age).
